lesson.title: The Map Behind Every Packet's Journey
lesson.summary: Routing is the process routers use to figure out, ahead of time, which path a packet should follow to reach a distant destination across a network of interconnected links.
lesson.body:
Every time you load a webpage or send a message, your data crosses a chain of routers, each of which has to decide, in a fraction of a second, which direction to send it next. At the network layer, this handoff only works because routers have already done a huge amount of background work: they have talked to each other, mapped out which networks are reachable, and worked out good paths to each one. That background work, discovering the network's shape and computing paths through it, is what we call routing.

It helps to separate routing from the simpler, faster action of forwarding. Forwarding is what a router does to a single packet the instant it arrives: look at the destination address, check a table, and send the packet out the correct interface. Routing is the slower, ongoing process that builds and maintains that table in the first place. If forwarding is like a driver glancing at a road sign and turning, routing is like the mapmaking and signposting that had to happen long before the driver ever got there. A router that has no idea how to reach a destination has nothing correct to forward toward, no matter how fast its forwarding hardware is.

Routing has to solve a genuinely hard problem: a large network is a graph of routers and links, often with many possible paths between any two points, and the best path can change as links fail, get congested, or come back online. Routers exchange information about which networks they can reach and at what cost, using rules called routing algorithms and protocols, so that every router can build a table of good next hops. The rest of this chapter's concepts, routing tables, static and default routes, distance vector routing, and protocols like RIP, are all pieces of that machine: different ways of answering the same question, given everything I currently know about the network, what is the best next step toward each destination.
